Clean Energy in the Age of Data and AI: How Data and AI Are Reshaping Clean Energy and Development?

26 January marks the International Day of Clean Energy, a moment to reflect on how we deliver equitable and sustainable energy transitions that leave no one behind and protect our planet.

For every generation, energy progress has never been just about technology—it has been about expanding what people and societies are able to do. Steam turned heat into motion and powered the first industrial surge. Electricity multiplied development, bringing light to homes, power to industry, and refrigeration that keeps food and vaccines safe. Today, clean energy is becoming the backbone of a new development era—one increasingly shaped not only by electrons, but by data and artificial intelligence.

AI-enabled forecasting and optimisation can unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity without building new lines, delivering power to millions of people. In practice, better forecasting has already increased wind power value by up to 20% and reduced outage duration by as much as half in some systems.

But this impact is not automatic. Without deliberate design and governance, data and AI can deepen strain on energy systems. When used intentionally, they can strengthen access, resilience, and fairness, and help deliver a just energy transition.

So how do we maximise these gains without creating or entrenching a new digital and energy divide?

1️⃣ Energy data must be treated as public infrastructure
Open, trusted data on demand, grid capacity, and system performance reduces uncertainty and unlocks investment at scale. When data is shared, the benefits of AI and digital tools can move from pilots to systems.

2️⃣ AI and energy must operate within land, water, and social limits
Efficiency gains matter only if they respect resource constraints and local realities. Digital optimisation cannot come at the expense of people or ecosystems.

3️⃣ Al needs to deliver for people
The growth of energy, digital, and AI should be judged by whether intelligence expands access, resilience, and livelihoods, not just system performance.
The opportunities are real. Data and AI can accelerate the energy transition in ways we have never seen before. 

But only if they are governed deliberately, aligned with development goals, and designed to serve people first.
